slots.overviewDescription: htop in context: a person at a terminal, one C program, and the operating system it samples.
slots.mapDescription: The modules of the htop binary with the paths of startup, a refresh tick, drawing a frame, a keypress and a settings change.
slots.completionIntro: You followed htop from main into its one loop, watched a tick pull numbers out of the kernel into the process table and the meters, saw a frame drawn row by row, and traced a keypress down to a kill() call.
slots.completionLessons:
• The whole program is one loop in ScreenManager_run: sample if the delay passed, draw if needed, wait for a key
  • Core code calls Machine_scan, ProcessTable_goThroughEntries and Platform_*; exactly one platform directory is compiled in to provide them
  • "Classes" are structs whose first member is the parent struct, plus a const table of function pointers
  • Keys go to the focused panel first; actions answer with Htop_Reaction flags that the panel turns into a HandlerResult for the loop

panels.introHtml:
Start here

htop, an interactive process viewer

A map of htop-dev/htop for a newcomer who wants to contribute. htop is one C99 program with no threads and no services: it samples the operating system, keeps a table of processes in memory and draws it with ncurses.

The map favours the runtime: what happens on every refresh tick, on a keypress and when a frame is drawn, and which file holds each part.

htop is made by Hisham Muhammad and the htop dev team and released under the GPLv2 or later. This map is not affiliated with its authors.

Try it

  • Play A refresh tick, then Draw a frame: together they are one turn of the main loop.
  • Open Main loop or Platform layer and look inside for a code walkthrough with line links.
  • Open Project structure to see which files to read first.
panels.overviewHtml:
The full map

One binary, one loop

Every card inside the boundary is a group of .c files linked into the single htop binary. Nothing runs in parallel: ScreenManager_run is the only loop, and everything else is called from it.

How to read it

The person and the terminal are on the left, startup and the loop next to them, the in-memory data model and the header meters in the middle, and the platform layer and the kernel on the right. Arrows are function calls, labelled with the function to search for.

The Platform layer card stands for nine directories of which one is compiled in; Linux is used as the example throughout.

people.title: Person at a terminal
people.text: htop is interactive: one person, one terminal. It can also run for a fixed number of frames with -n.

term.title: Terminal
term.text: The terminal emulator or console htop runs in. htop talks to it almost entirely through the curses library.

start.title: Startup and settings
start.text: main is one line. CommandLine_run builds the model, the header, the main panel and the screen manager, runs the loop and saves the settings on the way out.

loop.title: Main loop and input
loop.line1: Sample, draw, wait for a key,
loop.text: The only loop in the program, the panel that shows the process list and receives keys, the key actions, and the extra screens they open.

model.title: Data model
model.text: What htop knows after a scan: host-wide numbers in Machine, rows in a Table, and a Process struct per process or thread.

meters.title: Header meters
meters.text: The header lays meters out in columns. Each meter class knows how to fetch its values and the generic meter code knows how to draw them as text, bar, graph or LED.

platform.title: Platform layer
platform.text: The code that knows how to ask this operating system for CPU, memory and processes. The core calls it through a fixed set of function names.

draw.title: Drawing and foundation
draw.text: The pieces everything else leans on: the curses wrapper and colour schemes, attributed strings, and the Object, Vector, Hashtable and XUtils helpers.

os.title: Operating system
os.text: Where the numbers come from and where signals go. On Linux that is mostly files under /proc and /sys.

nodes.what: Starts htop (or pcp-htop), reads the meters and the process list, and presses keys: arrows to move, F3 to search, F6 to sort, F9 to send a signal, F2 for Setup.
nodes.why: Everything in the program is paced by this person: the loop wakes up either because a key arrived or because the refresh delay ran out.
nodes.tools: Command-line flags are listed in printHelpFlag in CommandLine.c; the in-program key help is actionHelp in Action.c.

nodes.what: Displays what ncurses writes and sends key presses and mouse reports back as bytes on standard input.
nodes.why: htop has no other user interface. If the terminal goes away, the loop ends after 100 empty reads in a row that were not refresh timeouts.
nodes.tools: Reached only through the curses library (ProvideCurses.h picks the ncurses headers).

nodes.what: main in htop.c only calls CommandLine_run. That function parses the flags, initialises the platform, creates the machine, the process table, the settings, the header, the main panel and the screen manager, runs the loop, and on exit saves the settings and frees everything.
nodes.why: This is the one place where you can see every long-lived object being created and in which order. The style guide calls htop.c and pcp-htop.c the main entrance points into the code.
nodes.tools: htop.c · pcp-htop.c (the entry for the PCP build, which also sets up PMAPI options) · CommandLine.c

nodes.what: Holds every option: display flags, the refresh delay, colour scheme, the header layout with meter names per column, and a list of ScreenSettings (one per screen tab) with its columns, sort key, sort direction and tree mode. Reads htoprc at startup and writes it back on exit when changed is set.
nodes.why: Almost every module reads host->settings; settings->ss is the active screen and decides which columns are shown and how rows are sorted.

nodes.what: The configuration file. The path is $HTOPRC if set, otherwise $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/htop/htoprc when that variable is an absolute path, otherwise htop/htoprc under the home directory plus the build-time CONFIGDIR (/.config by default, /.pcp for the PCP build). If that cannot be read, the legacy ~/.htoprc (which is then migrated to the new location and deleted) and then the system-wide SYSCONFDIR/htoprc are tried before built-in defaults.
nodes.why: It is the only state htop keeps between runs, apart from the search and filter history file.
nodes.tools: Path logic in Settings_new (Settings.c). Written through a temporary file and rename.

nodes.what: ScreenManager_run is the program's only loop. Each turn it checks whether the refresh delay has passed and, if so, rescans the machine and the tables and updates the meters; redraws the header and its panels when something changed; then waits for a key in Panel_getCh and offers it to the focused panel. It also lays its panels out side by side and turns mouse clicks into events.
nodes.why: There is no timer and no second thread. The wait for a key has a timeout equal to the refresh delay, and that timeout is what makes the display update on its own.
nodes.tools: ScreenManager.c · ScreenManager_run, checkRecalculation, ScreenManager_drawPanels. Setup and the pickers create a second ScreenManager and run the same loop nested.

nodes.what: Panel is the generic scrolling list widget: a Vector of objects, a selection, scroll offsets, a header line and a function bar. Panel_draw renders each visible item by calling its class's display function. MainPanel is the Panel subclass that shows the process list; its event handler looks keys up in a table of actions and drives incremental search and filter (IncSet).
nodes.why: Keys are offered to the focused panel before the loop's own defaults, so each panel class decides what a key means. Every list on screen, from the process list to the Setup pages, is a Panel.
nodes.tools: Panel.c · MainPanel.c · IncSet.c (search and filter line) with History.c (its history file) · FunctionBar.c (the F1 to F10 labels on the bottom line) · ListItem.c

nodes.what: One small function per key: sort, tree view, tag, kill, renice, follow, pause, open Setup or an information screen. Action_setBindings fills the key table; each action receives the shared State and returns Htop_Reaction flags such as HTOP_REFRESH, HTOP_RECALCULATE, HTOP_SAVE_SETTINGS or HTOP_QUIT.
nodes.why: To add a key you write an action here and add one line to the binding table. The flags tell the caller what has to be redone, so most actions leave redrawing the main screen to the loop.
nodes.tools: Action.c, Action.h · platform-only keys are added by Platform_setBindings (on Linux: I/O priority and autogroup nice)

nodes.what: Everything that temporarily takes over the screen. Setup (CategoriesPanel plus the display options, header layout, meters, screens and colours panels) and the pickers (signals, sort column, user, affinity) are Panels run by a nested ScreenManager. The per-process information screens (environment, open files, locks, strace, command) derive from InfoScreen, which has its own small loop; the open-files and strace screens start lsof and strace (or truss) as child programs and show their output. The backtrace screen is different: a BacktracePanel run by a nested ScreenManager that has no header.
nodes.why: Setup panels edit Settings directly and set changed, which is how a choice ends up in htoprc.

nodes.what: The host as htop sees it: the settings pointer, timestamps of the current sample, total memory and swap, CPU counts, the users table, and the list of tables with the active one. Machine_scanTables runs the three scan phases (prepare, iterate, clean up) on every table. Machine_new, Machine_scan and Machine_delete are declared in Machine.h but implemented in the platform directory.
nodes.why: It is the hub the rest of the code reaches through: rows, tables and meters all hold a host pointer. The platform extends the struct (on Linux, LinuxMachine) with the values it sampled.
nodes.tools: Machine.c, Machine.h · UsersTable.c (uid to name cache via getpwuid). Unlike rows, tables, panels and meters, Machine is a plain struct, not an Object.

nodes.what: Table keeps all known rows in a Vector, a Hashtable from row id to row, and a display list in screen order. After a scan it drops rows that were not seen again; Table_rebuildPanel sorts or builds the tree, skips hidden and filtered rows, fills the main panel and restores the selection. ProcessTable is the subclass whose rows are processes: it adds task counters and hands the scan to the platform.
nodes.why: Scanning and showing are separate steps. A scan only updates rows; the panel is refilled from the table on every redraw, which is why a filter or a new sort order applies without rescanning.

nodes.what: Row is anything shown as a line in a table: id, parent, tagged, shown, tree state. Process extends it with the fields every platform has (user, command line, CPU and memory percent, nice, state) and the code that prints a field, compares two processes for sorting, builds the merged command string, and sends a signal or changes priority. Each platform extends it once more (LinuxProcess) for its own columns.
nodes.why: A column is a ProcessField enum value (platform-only ones are listed in the platform's ProcessField.h) handled in three places: the field table that names it, writeField that prints it and compareByKey that sorts by it.

nodes.what: The implementation of the functions the core calls but does not implement. On Linux: Platform.c (Platform_init, the list of meter classes, Platform_setCPUValues, Platform_setMemoryValues, load average, battery, disk and network I/O, extra key bindings), LinuxMachine.c (Machine_new, Machine_scan), LinuxProcessTable.c (ProcessTable_new, ProcessTable_goThroughEntries) and LinuxProcess.c (the Linux-only columns).
nodes.why: The build picks exactly one directory, so core code calls Platform_* with no run-time dispatch. Porting htop means writing these four source files, their headers and a ProcessField.h for a new system.
nodes.tools: linux/ (procfs and sysfs) · darwin/ (sysctl, Mach and libproc calls) · freebsd/, dragonflybsd/, netbsd/, openbsd/ (sysctl and libkvm) · solaris/ (kstat and procfs walking) · pcp/ (Performance Co-Pilot metrics through PMAPI, built as pcp-htop, with columns, meters and screens defined in config files) · unsupported/ (a stub with one fake process). generic/ and zfs/ hold code shared by several platforms. On Linux, optional libraries (libsensors for temperatures, libnl for delay accounting) are loaded at run time with dlopen. Selection: configure.ac sets my_htop_platform, Makefile.am adds that directory's sources.

nodes.what: The source of every number htop shows and the target of its actions. On Linux the platform layer reads text files such as /proc/stat, /proc/meminfo and the per-process /proc/PID/stat, statm and cmdline; signals and priorities go through kill and setpriority.
nodes.why: htop does not cache across runs and does not use a daemon (except in the PCP build, where the PCP collector is the source).

nodes.what: The area above the process list. It holds one Vector of meters per layout column, creates the meters named in the settings by looking the name up in Platform_meterTypes, asks every meter to update on each scan and to draw on each redraw, and computes its own height.
nodes.why: The header is updated on every scan even while the process list is paused, so graph meters have no gaps.

nodes.what: Meter.c has the generic part: the MeterClass function table and the four draw modes (text, bar, graph, LED). Each concrete meter (CPUMeter.c, MemoryMeter.c, LoadAverageMeter.c, TasksMeter.c and others) is a MeterClass instance with an updateValues function that fills values and a text buffer, usually by calling a Platform_* function.
nodes.why: A new meter is one file with a class definition plus one line in each platform's Platform_meterTypes list. Drawing comes for free.
nodes.tools: Meter.c, Meter.h, MeterMode.h · 15 concrete *Meter.c files at the top level, more in linux/, zfs/ and other platform directories · DynamicMeter.c for meters defined by config files (PCP)

nodes.what: Starts and stops curses (CRT_init, CRT_done), sets the input timeout with halfdelay(settings->delay), enables the keypad and the mouse, defines the colour schemes and exposes the active one as CRT_colors[element], and installs the crash handler that restores the terminal and prints a bug-report template to standard error, including the current settings.
nodes.why: It does not wrap drawing: panels and meters call curses functions such as mvhline and mvaddnstr directly and only take their attributes from CRT_colors.

nodes.what: A string in which every character carries its own colour and attributes. A row or a meter builds one by appending pieces (RichString_appendAscii, RichString_appendWide); the panel then writes it to the screen with curses' attributed-string call.
nodes.why: It separates what a line says from where it is drawn, so a row can be rendered without knowing its screen position or whether it is selected.
nodes.tools: RichString.c, RichString.h · wide-character or plain variant chosen at build time

nodes.what: Object.h defines the base of the class emulation: a struct holding a pointer to an ObjectClass with extends, display, delete and compare. Vector is a growable array of objects that can own and sort its items; Hashtable maps an integer key to a pointer. XUtils wraps allocation (xMalloc, xCalloc, xStrdup) and string helpers (String_eq, String_startsWith, xSnprintf).
nodes.why: The x allocators never return NULL: on failure they restore the terminal and abort, so callers do not check. Subclasses add function pointers by embedding the parent class struct first (RowClass, PanelClass, MeterClass, TableClass).

startup.title: Startup
startup.desc: From typing htop to the first turn of the loop: everything long-lived is built once, in CommandLine_run.

hops.t: The person runs htop. main in htop.c does nothing but return CommandLine_run(argc, argv).

After parseArguments, Platform_init runs; on Linux it checks that /proc is readable and detects whether htop runs in a container. Then Machine_new and ProcessTable_new are called: both are implemented in the platform directory and return the platform's larger structs (LinuxMachine, LinuxProcessTable).
hops.note: A users table and the dynamic meter, column and screen tables are created just before; only the PCP build fills the dynamic ones; on Linux the platform returns NULL for them, and the column table is then replaced by an empty one.

hops.t: Settings_new(host, dm, dc, ds) fills in the defaults in code, then looks for a configuration file.
Settings_read parses htoprc line by line. If it cannot be read, the legacy ~/.htoprc and the system-wide htoprc are tried; if none can be read, default meters and default screens are created instead.

Machine_populateTablesFromSettings attaches the process table to every screen that has no table of its own. Header_new and Header_populateFromSettings create one meter per name in the settings, matching names against Platform_meterTypes.

Flags from the command line override the loaded settings (delay, tree view, sort key, colours). CRT_init then starts curses, sets halfdelay(settings->delay), enables the keypad, installs signal handlers and loads the colour scheme.

MainPanel_new builds the main panel and its key table, a State struct ties host, panel and header together, and the panel is added to a new ScreenManager. After one priming Machine_scan and Machine_scanTables, ScreenManager_run takes over until the person quits.
hops.note: When it returns: Platform_done, CRT_done, Settings_write if anything changed, then everything is freed.

tick.title: A refresh tick
tick.desc: No key arrives within the delay: the loop samples the machine, rescans the processes, updates the meters and refills the panel.

hops.t: The loop is waiting in Panel_getCh, which calls curses getch(). Because of halfdelay(settings->delay), it gives up after delay tenths of a second (15 by default, so 1.5 s) and returns ERR. The loop goes round again.
hops.note: The same path runs right after a key press, but then the scan is skipped unless the delay has passed or the key asked for a rescan.

hops.t: checkRecalculation reads the clock. If more than delay tenths have passed since the last scan (or a key asked for a rescan, or the clock went backwards), it marks the active table for sorting and calls Machine_scan(host).
hops.note: No sort is requested while updates are paused. After a key that falls through to the panel's default scrolling handler, sorting is held back for a few turns, except in tree view.

hops.t: Machine_scan is the platform's function. In linux/LinuxMachine.c it scans memory, zswap, huge pages, ZFS ARC, zram and CPU times, plus CPU frequency when that option or the CPU temperature option is on.
On Linux these are reads of /proc/meminfo, /proc/stat and similar files. The results land in fields of LinuxMachine such as usedMem, cachedMem and the per-CPU cpuData.
Unless updates are paused (the Z key), Machine_scanTables runs next: for every table it calls Table_scanPrepare, Table_scanIterate and Table_scanCleanup, which dispatch through the table's class.
Prepare: ProcessTable_prepareEntries zeroes the task counters and Table_prepareEntries marks every existing row updated = false, show = true.
Iterate: ProcessTable_iterateEntries does one thing, it calls the platform's ProcessTable_goThroughEntries.

On Linux, LinuxProcessTable_recurseProcTree lists /proc, opens every numeric directory, recurses into its task directory for threads, and reads statm, stat and, depending on the columns in use, more files.

ProcessTable_getProcess finds the row by PID in the table's hashtable or constructs a new LinuxProcess. The fields are filled in, CPU percent is computed from the change in user plus system time over the sample period, a new process is added with ProcessTable_add, and the row is marked updated = true.

Clean up: ProcessTable_cleanupEntries rebuilds each command string and removes rows that were not updated, because their process is gone. With "highlight changes" on, such a row, if it was shown, stays as a tombstone for highlightDelaySecs first.
Back in checkRecalculation, Header_updateData runs. It runs even when updates are paused, so graphs keep moving. If the header height changed, the panels are resized.
For each meter in each column, Meter_updateValues calls the class's updateValues function pointer.

Example: MemoryMeter_updateValues calls Platform_setMemoryValues, which copies the numbers Machine_scan stored in LinuxMachine into the meter's values array, adjusting them for ZFS ARC and zswap; the meter then formats its text buffer.
The scan set redraw, so Table_rebuildPanel(host->activeTable) runs: Table_updateDisplayList, when needsSort is set, sorts the rows with the class's compare function, or builds the tree in tree view.
The panel is emptied with Panel_prune and refilled with Panel_set for every row that is shown and not filtered out. Selection and scroll position are restored, or moved to the followed process.

tick.ending: The data is fresh and the panel holds the right rows. Draw a frame shows what happens next in the same turn of the loop.

draw.title: Draw a frame
draw.desc: After a scan or a handled key: the header meters and the panels are drawn through curses.

hops.t: At the end of checkRecalculation, when redraw is set and the meters are not hidden, Header_draw runs.

The header blanks its lines, then calls meter->draw(meter, x, y, width) for each meter, column by column. draw was set by Meter_setMode to the text, bar, graph or LED routine in Meter.c, unless the meter class brings its own.
hops.note: The draw routines write with curses calls such as attrset and mvaddnstr, taking attributes from CRT_colors. Text mode asks the meter class's display function to build a RichString.

hops.t: ScreenManager_drawPanels draws the screen tabs when enabled, then calls Panel_draw for each of its panels.
On a forced redraw the column header is rebuilt by Table_printHeader. When the panel needs a redraw, each visible item gets Object_display(item, &richString); for a process that is Row_display.
hops.note: When only the selection moved, just the old and the new selected lines are drawn.

hops.t: Row_display walks the active screen's fields and calls the class's writeField for each. LinuxProcess_rowWriteField prints the Linux-only columns and passes the rest to Process_writeField. Each call appends coloured text to the RichString.

The panel clears the line with mvhline and writes the finished string with curses' attributed-string call (a second call when pinned columns are on), using the selection colour for the selected row. Then it draws the function bar on the last line.
Nothing in the loop calls refresh(). The frame reaches the terminal when the loop next waits in getch().
hops.note: That getch() refreshes the screen first is curses behaviour; it is not visible in htop's code.

kill.title: A keypress: F9 sends a signal
kill.desc: One key from the terminal to a kill() call and back to a redraw, through the panel's key table and a nested loop for the signal picker.

hops.t: The person selects a process and presses F9.
The terminal sends an escape sequence. Because CRT_init enabled keypad mode, curses hands it over as the single code KEY_F(9).
The focused panel was waiting in Panel_getCh; its getch() call now returns the key instead of timing out.
Back in ScreenManager_run, the key is not ERR, so redraw is set and Panel_eventHandler(panelFocus, ch) is called, which for the main panel is MainPanel_eventHandler.
No search or filter is being typed, so the handler runs this->keys[ch](this->state). Action_setBindings put actionKill at KEY_F(9) and at k.
actionKill returns at once in read-only mode or on a screen that does not show processes. Otherwise it builds a SignalsPanel: a plain Panel listing the platform's signals.

Action_pickFromVector creates a second ScreenManager with the signal list on the left and the main panel beside it, and runs the same loop nested. Ticks keep happening, and the selected process is followed so the selection stays on it.
hops.note: Enter ends the nested loop: the default Panel handler returns BREAK_LOOP.

hops.t: With a signal chosen, the header shows "Sending..." and MainPanel_foreachRow calls Process_rowSendSignal on every tagged row, or on the selected row when none is tagged.
Process_sendSignal is one line: kill(Process_getPid(this), sgn.i).
actionKill returns HTOP_REFRESH | HTOP_REDRAW_BAR | HTOP_UPDATE_PANELHDR.
MainPanel_eventHandler translates the reaction into a HandlerResult: HANDLED | REFRESH | REDRAW. The loop clears the sort hold-off and forces a full redraw on its next turn.

kill.ending: The signalled process is still listed. It disappears on a later tick, when the scan no longer finds it and cleanup removes its row.

setup.title: Change a setting and keep it
setup.desc: F2 opens Setup in a nested loop; a changed option sets a flag, and the flag makes htop write htoprc when it exits.

hops.t: The person presses F2 (or S, or C).
The loop passes KEY_F(2) to MainPanel_eventHandler.
The key table holds actionSetup, which calls Action_runSetup.
Action_runSetup creates a new ScreenManager that shares the header and runs ScreenManager_run(scr, NULL, NULL, "Setup").
CategoriesPanel_new adds the category list as the left panel. Selecting a category removes the other panels and builds that page: display options, header layout, meters, screens or colours.
hops.note: A sixth page, screen tabs, exists only in the PCP build.

hops.t: Toggling an item in DisplayOptionsPanel changes the field in Settings and sets settings->changed = true. The panel also recalculates the header so the effect is visible at once.
Leaving Setup ends the nested loop. If settings changed, Action_runSetup copies the header's meters back with Header_writeBackToSettings. actionSetup returns a reaction that includes HTOP_RESIZE.
The main panel reports RESIZE, REDRAW and REFRESH; the outer loop lays the panels out again and redraws everything.
Much later, when the person quits and ScreenManager_run returns, CommandLine_run checks settings->changed and calls Settings_write(settings, false).

Settings_write writes to a temporary file next to htoprc and renames it over the old file. Nothing is written when writeConfig is false, which Settings_read sets when the existing file is not a regular file owned by and writable for the user, or cannot be opened for writing.

buildSteps.title: A program at a terminal
buildSteps.text: A one-line main, a startup function and the helpers every file uses: the Object base, Vector, Hashtable and the x-allocators.
buildSteps.decision: Classes are emulated with structs and const tables of function pointers, so plain C99 gets virtual methods without a framework.

buildSteps.title: A loop that draws lists
buildSteps.text: Start curses, show a scrolling Panel, and wait for a key with a timeout.
buildSteps.decision: The input timeout doubles as the refresh timer, so one thread and one loop are enough.

buildSteps.title: Something to show
buildSteps.text: A Machine, a table of rows and a Process per PID, configured by settings read from htoprc.
buildSteps.decision: Scanning fills the table; the panel is refilled from the table on every redraw. Filters and sorting never need a rescan.

buildSteps.title: Ask the operating system
buildSteps.text: Implement Machine_scan and ProcessTable_goThroughEntries for one system.
buildSteps.decision: One platform directory is chosen at configure time and linked in; the core calls fixed function names with no run-time dispatch.

buildSteps.title: Keys that do things
buildSteps.text: A table from key code to action, and the extra screens actions open.
buildSteps.decision: Actions return flags instead of redrawing; the loop decides what to recompute.

buildSteps.title: Meters on top
buildSteps.text: A header with columns of meters, each with an updateValues function and a shared set of draw modes.
buildSteps.decision: Many meters read what the machine scan already collected; the rest ask the platform layer when they update.

tour.title: One program between a person and the kernel
body: htop is a single C program. A person watches it in a terminal; it reads statistics from the operating system and can send signals back.
Inside are six parts: startup and settings, the main loop, the data model, the header meters, the platform layer, and the drawing helpers.
tour.why: There are about 170 files at the top level, but they fall into these few groups, and only one loop connects them.

tour.title: Everything is built once
body: Follow CommandLine_run: platform, machine, process table, settings, header, curses, main panel, then the loop.
tour.why: The order matters: settings need the machine, the header needs the settings, and curses starts late so that errors before it print normally.

tour.title: The timeout is the timer
body: Waiting for a key gives up after the refresh delay. The loop then samples machine-wide numbers through the platform layer.
tour.why: Machine_scan is declared in the core and implemented in the platform directory. That is the pattern for every platform call.

tour.title: Rescan the processes
body: Prepare marks every row as not seen, the platform walks the process list and updates or creates rows, cleanup removes the ones that were not seen.
tour.why: Rows persist between scans, which is how CPU percent can be computed from the difference to the previous sample.

tour.title: Meters, then the panel
body: Meters pull their values from what the scan stored. The table is sorted or turned into a tree and the visible rows are put into the panel.
tour.why: Scanning and showing are separate, so a filter or a different sort key takes effect on the next redraw without touching the kernel.

tour.title: A frame, line by line
body: The header draws its meters, the panel asks each row to render itself into a RichString, and curses sends the result to the terminal.
tour.why: Rows and meters draw themselves through function pointers in their class, so the panel and the header stay generic.

tour.title: A key becomes an action
body: F9 travels from the terminal through the focused panel's handler to an action, which opens a picker in a nested loop and finally calls kill().
tour.why: Two result types are in play: actions return Htop_Reaction, panel handlers return HandlerResult. MainPanel translates between them.

tour.title: A setting that survives
body: Setup edits the Settings struct in place and sets a changed flag; the file is written once, at exit.
tour.why: If htop is ended by a signal (SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGQUIT) instead of the quit key, the handler exits without writing htoprc.

tour.title: All of htop on one map

recap.people: A person runs it and presses keys.
recap.term: The terminal shows frames and delivers input.
recap.loop: One loop: sample, draw, wait, dispatch.
recap.model: Machine, tables and a row per process.
recap.platform: One OS directory supplies the scan functions.
recap.os: The kernel answers and receives signals.

body: To change behaviour on a key, start in Action.c. To add a column, look at Process.c and the platform's ProcessField.h. To add a meter, copy a small one such as MemoryMeter.c.
When in doubt, set a breakpoint in ScreenManager_run and step: every path on this map starts there.

main.title: Inside startup: CommandLine_run
main.sub: What CommandLine_run in CommandLine.c does between main and exit, in order.
main.cap: Read this function first. Every long-lived object is created here, in dependency order, and destroyed here. Nothing else in the program allocates the machine, the settings or the header.

steps.t: Set the locale and parse flags
steps.d: parseArguments fills a CommandLineSettings struct; only the read-only flag is applied at once.

exit.when: help, version or a bad flag

ScreenManager_run returns when the loop ends, normally because the person quit.

loop.title: Inside the main loop: ScreenManager_run
loop.sub: One turn of the while (!quit) loop in ScreenManager.c. Setup and the pickers run this same function on a second ScreenManager.
loop.cap: There is no separate timer. Step 3 blocks for at most the refresh delay; an empty read sends the loop back to step 1, where the clock decides whether to scan. A key press reaches step 6 and sets redraw, so the next turn redraws without necessarily rescanning.

steps.d: checkRecalculation: if the delay passed or a rescan was requested, run Machine_scan, Machine_scanTables (unless paused) and Header_updateData. If redraw is set, run Table_rebuildPanel and Header_draw. Skipped when this ScreenManager has no header.
Only when redraw or force_redraw is set.
Panel_getCh on the focused panel; returns ERR on timeout.

Only when built with mouse support and the mouse is enabled. A click becomes a function-bar key, a meter click, a column-header click, a screen-tab click or a row selection; the wheel becomes scroll keys.
Count down the sort hold-off, clear redraw and start the next turn.

exit.when: 100 empty reads in a row that were not timeouts

steps.t: Offer the key to the focused panel
steps.d: Panel_eventHandler(panelFocus, ch) returns a HandlerResult bit set.
REFRESH clears the sort hold-off, REDRAW forces a full redraw, RESIZE lays the panels out again, RESCAN requests a scan on the next turn. HANDLED ends the turn.

Terminal resize, left and right to change the focused panel when there are at least two, # to hide the meters, Esc, q or F10 to quit. Anything else goes to Panel_onKey for scrolling, and the sort hold-off is set to 5 turns.

keys.title: Inside the main panel: one key
keys.sub: What MainPanel_eventHandler in MainPanel.c does with a key before the loop's defaults see it.
keys.cap: Actions speak Htop_Reaction (Action.h); the loop understands HandlerResult (Panel.h). The last step is the translation between the two, and it is also where HTOP_SAVE_SETTINGS sets settings->changed.

steps.d: Any real key shows the selection bar again; an up, down or page key stops following a process unless sticky follow is on.
Sort by that column, or invert the order if it is already the sort key. In tree view sorted always by PID, the click leaves tree view and sorts by the column.
The key goes to IncSet_handleKey. A changed filter is stored in the active table and takes effect on the next panel rebuild.
Hide the selection bar and stop following.
this->keys[ch](this->state): the table filled by Action_setBindings and Platform_setBindings.
Digits typed in a row select the process with that PID.

steps.t: Turn the reaction into a result
steps.d: HTOP_REDRAW_BAR updates the function-bar labels here; HTOP_RESIZE, HTOP_UPDATE_PANELHDR, HTOP_REFRESH and HTOP_RECALCULATE become RESIZE, REDRAW, REFRESH and RESCAN.

scan.title: Inside the platform layer: the Linux process scan
scan.sub: What ProcessTable_goThroughEntries and LinuxProcessTable_recurseProcTree in linux/LinuxProcessTable.c do for every process on each tick. Other platforms implement the same function with their own system calls.
scan.cap: The cost of a tick is this loop times the number of tasks, so expensive files are read only when a visible column needs them: each column sets bits in ss->flags, and the scan checks those bits.

steps.d: Check whether autogroup is enabled if that column is shown, shift the GPU time counters, then recurse from PROCDIR.
Only entries whose name starts with a digit are processes (or, inside task, threads).
ProcessTable_getProcess with LinuxProcess_new as constructor; record the thread group.
Only for main tasks.

A row seen before that the settings hide is marked updated and not shown without reading any file. Hidden kernel and userland threads are still counted in the task totals; a hidden container process is not.

Memory sizes, state, times, parent, tty. Between the two, maps is read now and then when the library-size column or the deleted-library highlight needs it. CPU percent is the change in utime + stime divided by the sample period; memory percent is resident size over total memory.

exit.t: A new row is deleted, a known row is kept

steps.d: Look up the user, and compare the PID namespace with htop's own to tell whether the process runs in a container.
A new process gets its cmdline and comm read and is added to the table. Known processes re-read them only when "update process names" is on.
cgroup, smaps, I/O counters, delay accounting, OOM score, I/O priority, security attributes, working directory, autogroup, scheduling policy, GPU time.
updated = true, update the thread and task counters, and decide show from the hide settings.

structs.title: Inside the data model: the structs
structs.sub: There is no database. These C structs are the state between two ticks; a subclass embeds its parent as its first member, called super.
structs.cap: The inheritance chain for one line of the process list on Linux is Object, Row, Process, LinuxProcess. The same row sits in three containers of its table at once: the rows vector, the table hashtable and the displayList.

entries.t: The main loop: ScreenManager_run and checkRecalculation.
entries.why: Almost every runtime path starts here (the information screens have their own small loop). A breakpoint in ScreenManager_run is the fastest way to see htop work.
